deep_why: The core task is filling in missing and incorrect product information by comparing against brand reference data. The method works because when you check a noisy record against a trusted source simultaneously—both repairing errors and matching category—you avoid compounding mistakes that happen when you fix one thing, then discover the fix breaks the match. The brand knowledge base acts as ground truth; if your product name and attributes diverge from it, they're likely wrong. This principle holds because brand metadata is curated and consistent within a single seller's view. By doing both tasks at once through an agent, you respect the fact that product identity and product details are intertwined—fixing the name might reveal the brand, which then constrains what attributes are valid.

The goal is ranking items fairly across popularity tiers so unpopular-but-relevant items get shown despite having fewer interaction examples. The method learns specialized item selectors and combines them through learned gating, which works because you can decompose the problem: one expert learns what makes an item relevant given its own signals, while another emphasizes items most informative for learning user taste. The gating network then weighs these two paths based on the user and context. This is sound because relevance and informativeness are genuinely different objectives—an unpopular item can be highly relevant to one user but teach you little about users in general. By maintaining separate specialists and blending their predictions, you avoid a single scoring function that must simultaneously optimize both, which would necessarily trade off one for the other.

Fact-checking complex claims requires verifying sub-claims, but the challenge is that sub-claims depend on each other—the truth of one constrains whether others make sense. Rather than checking each piece independently, this method models the dependency graph between them, which is sound because reasoning in the real world is causal and sequential. If sub-claim A must be true for sub-claim B to be sensible, checking them in isolation loses that constraint. By scheduling verification to respect dependencies—confirming foundational claims first, then using those results to inform later checks—the method mirrors how humans actually reason through complex arguments. Intermediate results from early verifications become context for later ones, preventing the error cascade that happens when you verify pieces out of logical order.

The goal is capturing how places feel through multisensory and contextual data tied to personality traits. The method collects and visualizes this by letting people contribute sensory tags and photos tied to locations, then linking those tags to individual traits. This works because a place's sensory character is genuinely subjective—the same street smells different to different people based on attention and sensitivity. By collecting both the sensory impressions AND personality profiles, you build a model that acknowledges this: two observers rating the same place differently is not noise, it's signal about how context and trait interact. The visualization then lets you query both place and person, seeing that location X feels calm to introverts but energetic to sensation-seekers, which is the true pattern underlying recommendation.

The task is ranking knowledge-graph entities in conversation, balancing relevance to the current question with conversation history. The method constructs a local sub-graph around each candidate and computes many fine-grained relevance scores—lexical match, semantic similarity, dialog-aware signals—then combines them through graph layers that let information flow. This works because relevance in conversation has multiple dimensions that don't reduce to a single score: the entity might match the question lexically but violate the prior dialog context, or vice versa. By keeping signals separate and letting graph operations propagate them, you let the model learn which signals matter most for THIS entity in THIS context. The graph structure itself encodes the knowledge-graph relationships, so propagating scores through those edges means you're ranking entities partly on what they connect to, not just their direct match.

Misinformation detection must model both how people actually judge credibility and the linguistic patterns that exploit that judgment. The method measures real user believability ratings and simultaneously analyzes linguistic ambivalence—mixed emotional and temporal cues within claims. This is sound because the psychology is bidirectional: people are fooled by specific language patterns, AND those patterns leave traces in the text itself. By using both signals together in a graph model, you're saying: this text is suspicious partly because its language is internally inconsistent (emotion mixed with facts, future tense mixing with present), and partly because people marked it as dubious in practice. Neither signal alone is reliable—language mixing could be honest nuance—but together they sharply distinguish misinformation from legitimate reporting.

Click prediction uses multiple parallel sub-networks to capture different feature interactions, but a naive approach amplifies noise as interactions layer on top of each other. The method gives each sub-network its own specialized embeddings and uses gating to select which layer-wise combinations to actually use. This works because feature interactions at different depths genuinely matter differently: early interactions capture obvious patterns, later ones capture subtle ones, but not all paths through the network reduce noise equally. By decoupling embeddings, each sub-network builds a different view of the same features, and gating learns which refined views to trust at each layer. This avoids the cumulative error of standard layered designs where wrong interactions from layer N propagate into layer N+1, because you're actively filtering which paths to combine.

Large language models inherit biases from their training data, but the question is whether this happens because the data itself is systematically biased or for other reasons. The method measures political lean directly in a web corpus across many topics using statistical rigor. This is sound because if the corpus is left-leaning, any model trained on it will absorb that asymmetry—not through active bias in training, but passively, because the input distribution itself is skewed. By measuring the corpus carefully and then training models and observing their outputs, you can trace the causal path: biased data produces biased models. This is crucial because it means you cannot fix the model problem without addressing the source. The statistical rigor matters because small biases in the data compound into large ones in the model.

Query expansion aims to enrich a search question with diverse context, but adding random related content dilutes relevance. This method uses multiple agents in conversation: one asks clarifying sub-questions, another answers them from different angles, a third filters out weak answers. This works because good expansion is not just adding words, but adding diverse-yet-relevant context, which mimics how humans think through a complex question. A Socratic questioning agent generates sub-questions that each illuminate a different facet of the original intent. The answering agent elaborates on each facet, and the feedback agent ensures you keep only the elaborations that genuinely deepen retrieval, discarding tangents. By chaining these, you get expansions that are both broad and focused, unlike single-pass expansion which typically drifts into noise.

This is a position paper on future directions rather than a methodological contribution. The core insight is that future assistants will integrate multiple abilities—seeing across images, video, and audio; reasoning over long chains; personalizing to individual users—into a single unified model. This is powerful because each ability has historically required separate systems, creating brittle pipelines that lose information at handoffs. A unified model that handles all modalities and reasoning styles simultaneously can make connections that specialists miss, and personalization becomes not a post-processing step but integral to all inference. The gain comes from end-to-end optimization: the model learns to emphasize different signals for different users, without forced abstraction layers between perception and reasoning.

Citation networks are typically sparse in certain metadata fields, making it hard to classify authors or cluster related researchers. This method uses language models to generate descriptive text for sparse fields, then encodes this text into features for the network. This works because sparse fields contain implicit information that a language model can make explicit. For example, an author affiliation is just a name, but an LLM can write a paragraph about that institution's research area, which carries much more signal. These descriptions, encoded by a linguistic model, become dense features that connect related entities more clearly in the network. By augmenting the network structure with generated context, you enrich the input signal without changing the downstream model, so any existing network method immediately benefits. The chain-of-thought validation helps ensure the text is factually grounded rather than hallucinated.

Conversational entity retrieval from knowledge graphs must handle multi-turn context—what was asked before constrains which entity answers the current question. The method builds local neighborhoods around candidate entities and models relevance signals using graph operations and attention to conversation history. This is sound because entity identity in a knowledge graph is defined by its connections: what it points to, what points to it, and what it's labeled as. In conversation, the same entity can be the right answer to different questions depending on what was discussed. By propagating relevance signals through the graph structure itself and conditioning on dialog history, you're saying: the right entity is one whose connections align with both the current query AND the prior context. Graph operations naturally capture this because they respect the structure of how entities relate.

News recommendation requires modeling relationships between articles, but articles often contain exaggerated or biased language that distorts these relationships. The method uses a multimodal model (with images) to learn what the articles actually mean, then distills this understanding into a text-only model so it can extract factual triples. This is sound because images provide ground truth that text alone cannot: a photo of an event is harder to misrepresent than a written description. By learning from images first, the model absorbs a debiased understanding of the underlying facts. Distillation then teaches a text-only model to extract the same factual meaning from text alone, effectively teaching it to read around the exaggeration. The permutation-invariant training and preference alignment ensure the extracted triples are consistent and objective across variations, so recommendation is based on what actually happened, not on rhetorical framing.

This is a workshop call rather than a research contribution; it addresses the broader question of how generative models are reshaping recommendation and search systems. The core observation is that recent semantic encoders and large language models can incorporate textual and visual meaning into recommendation in new ways, enabling systems to reason over content semantics rather than just user-item interactions. This matters because traditional recommendation was pattern-based—find users similar to you, recommend what they liked—but semantic understanding lets systems recommend based on meaning: even if no one like you has rated something, the system can reason that this article's topic, tone, and perspective aligns with your interests. The integration of generative and discriminative models lets systems both retrieve relevant candidates and generate explanations for why they matter.

Regression on imbalanced tabular data deployed online faces distribution shift: the training data emphasizes certain value ranges, and the test distribution is unpredictable and shifts over time. The method partitions the feature space into regions using a statistical mixture model, trains specialists for each region, and adapts at test time by re-weighting specialists based on incoming features. This works because imbalance in regression means some value ranges are underrepresented in training, leaving specialists for those ranges undertrained. By identifying regions explicitly and training separately, you ensure each region has expert coverage. Crucially, test-time adaptation works because the feature distribution tells you which regions incoming data lives in, and you can upweight the corresponding experts without retraining. This is sound because the regional structure is stable—even if the target distribution shifts, the feature space structure remains valid, and you can use it to quickly adjust specialist weights to match new data.
